extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, inventors studying U.S. patent subject-matter
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what kinds of inventions qualify as patentable subject-matter under U.S. law (constitutional/statutory basis, statutory classes, and the distinction between patentable processes and unpatentable principles/laws of nature), illustrated by leading cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and statutory foundation of the patent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has power to promote the progress of science and useful arts by securing for limited times to inventors the exclusive right to their discoveries (U.S. Constitution, Art. I, §8). Section 4886 of the Revised Statutes (as amended) provides that persons who have invented or discovered any new and useful art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to conditions and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional grant is the legal foundation for U.S. patentability rules; statutory language (four classes) defines the categories of patentable subject-matter. Historical variations of conditions/limitations are noted but the core statute lists the four categories that determine eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'discovery' in patent law
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Constitution and statute, the word 'discovery' means invention; it does not carry its broad dictionary meaning. The 'discoveries' of inventors are inventions; laws of nature or geographical discoveries are not patentable as 'discoveries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents reward inventions (created things) not findings of pre-existing natural facts. Examples: discovering an island or a law of nature is not patentable; a patent must claim invention (an art, machine, manufacture, or composition) or an improvement thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four statutory classes of patentable subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents may be granted for arts (processes), machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter (and improvements thereof). These things are created by original thought rather than merely found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing subject-matter eligibility, map the invention to one of these four classes; the text emphasizes that these are creations (inventions) not discoveries of existing natural facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent law meaning of 'art' (process) and classification of processes
rubrics_metrics.description: In patent law 'art' has a narrower meaning equivalent to certain kinds of 'process.' Processes are classified: (1) operations involving heat, light, electricity, magnetism, chemical action, pneumatics, hydraulics, or other forces producing chemical change; (2) operations entirely mechanical and only the peculiar functions of respective machines constructed to perform them; (3) operations entirely mechanical that may be performed by hand or by various mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settled holdings: processes of the first class are patentable; processes of the second class are unpatentable in the United States; processes of the third class have been held patentable. A process need not involve chemical change — new mechanical readjustments or new juxtaposition of parts can suffice to make a process patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods/systems are not patentable subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'system' or method of transacting business is neither an 'art' nor within any other designation of patentable subject-matter; e.g., a system of cash registering and checking for hotels apart from physical means is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the abstract system is not patentable, the physical means of carrying out a system may be patentable in principle; however, such patents historically have not fared well in court. Assess whether the claim is merely an abstract system or claims concrete physical implementing means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature, scientific principles, and facts are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles, scientific facts, and laws of nature are intangible mental conceptions and are not material substances; they are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent cannot claim a law of nature itself; however, an invention (process or apparatus) that applies or utilizes a law of nature may be patentable. The critical distinction is whether the claim effectively monopolizes the law/principle (unpatentable) or claims a concrete application/process (potentially patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between a process and a principle governs claim validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a particular patent is for a process or for a principle (law of nature) can determine its validity; claims that are for principles rather than concrete processes or apparatus may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To decide validity, analyze if the claim is seeking to appropriate a principle/law of nature (impermissible) or is a claim to a concrete method/apparatus applying that principle. The text recommends examining controlling cases to derive the rule that underlies them all.

rubrics_metrics.name: McClurg v. Kingsland (illustration of patentable process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harley's method of imparting rotary motion to molten metal by injecting it tangentially into a mould produced the desired result and was held by the Supreme Court to be a patent for a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This case illustrates that a practical method of applying known natural forces (centrifugal force) by a specific mechanical technique can be a patentable process, not merely a claim to the force or principle itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Reilly v. Morse (illustration of unpatentable principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Morse's eighth claim, construed as a claim for the use of an electric current for marking intelligible signs at any distance, was held void by the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This decision exemplifies that claims which effectively claim the use of a broad natural principle (here, the electric current for conveying intelligence) without limiting to concrete means or methods are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mowry v. Whitney (illustration of patentable process utilizing laws of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitney's process for treating cast-iron wheels — chilling rims, then reheating in a furnace to equalize temperatures and cool slowly so as to achieve hardened rims and annealed hubs — was held to be a valid process patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that exploiting knowledge of natural phenomena (thermal expansion/contraction) via a specific multi-stage process can be patentable; the claim was to a concrete sequence of operations, not to the natural law alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tilghman v. Proctor (illustration of patentable chemical process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tilghman obtained a patent for manufacturing fat acids and glycerine from fatty bodies by action of water at high temperature and pressure; the Supreme Court held the patent to be for a process and valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example that processes applying chemical knowledge (Chevreul's discoveries) using specified conditions and apparatus can constitute patentable subject-matter when claimed as a process.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Telephone Cases / Bell (process and apparatus claims can be patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell's invention — mounting diaphragms on armatures and transmitting sounds by electrical undulations similar to air vibrations — was held to be a patent for a process as well as for an apparatus, and the process claim was valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that a novel apparatus with an associated process of application (transmitting speech by electrical undulations) can be protected; claims should tie the application of known physical laws to concrete structures and steps.
